source: Marjieh, Sucholutsky, van Rijn, Jacoby, Griffiths (2023) Large language models predict human sensory judgments across six modalities
finding: GPT models give colour similarity and colour naming that track humans. GPT-4, given the same hex codes, names colours differently in Russian and English, in the direction of the known Russian light-blue versus dark-blue split.
numbers: Naming agreement with human maps: English GPT-4 0.59 (CI 0.56-0.63), GPT-3.5 0.50, GPT-3 0.39. Russian GPT-4 0.54, GPT-3.5 0.50, GPT-3 0.35. Lab ceiling 0.73-0.75. Human data: 103 English and 51 Russian speakers.
limits: Colour naming is lexical categorisation, not Slobin-style message encoding. Only naming is affected; no attention or memory measure. Authors read it as language reshaping perception, which over-reaches for a text-only model.
agent_relevance: Closest machine echo of a Whorf-type effect: prompt language alone shifts a model's category boundaries.

source: Marjieh, Sucholutsky, van Rijn, Jacoby, Griffiths (2023) Large language models predict human sensory judgments across six modalities (Russian blues detail)
finding: Dominant-category counts over Munsell chips match the Russian pattern. Siniy (dark blue) was dominant for 18 chips in GPT-4 and 29 in humans. Goluboy (light blue) for 33 and 26. Violet 27 and 32. Lilac 20 and 18. GPT-4 over-used turquoise.
numbers: Turquoise dominant for 46 chips in GPT-4 versus 15 in humans. English-to-Russian agreement drop for GPT-4 is 0.59 to 0.54, and GPT-3 0.39 to 0.35.
limits: Models do not match the human counts exactly. The Russian prompt costs a little fidelity.
agent_relevance: A non-English prompt can cost a few points of fidelity even on a native-language task.

source: Wendler, Veselovsky, Monea, West (2024) Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
finding: Logit lens on Llama-2 (7B, 13B, 70B) shows three phases. Middle layers already decode the right concept, but give it higher probability in English than in the input language. Final layers move to the input language. Authors say the concept space is closer to English.
numbers: Word sets: 139 Chinese, 104 German, 56 French, 115 Russian words. Tasks: translation, repetition, cloze, each with one correct single-token answer. Error bars are 95 percent Gaussian intervals.
limits: Single-token tasks, Llama-2 only. Not a behavioural test of different thought by language.
agent_relevance: Nearest mechanistic parallel to thinking for speaking: pick the concept first, then pick the surface language last. The pivot is English, not the speaker's language.
quote: intermediate embeddings ... give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language

source: Wendler, Veselovsky, Monea, West (2024) Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers (task design)
finding: Three tasks force one correct next token: translate, repeat, cloze. English rises before the target token in translation and cloze. In repetition, Chinese rises alongside English. The picture holds across the three model sizes.
numbers: French, German, Russian to Chinese translation and Chinese repetition and cloze; 7B, 13B and 70B.
limits: Single-token design cannot extend to full sentences without losing control.
agent_relevance: Gives a probe design to test whether a restate step moves the model's internal language.

source: Schut, Gal, Farquhar (2025) Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
finding: Logit lens on Llama-3.1-70B and others in French, German, Dutch and Mandarin. For meaning-bearing words the model first emits English-close representations, then translates. Steering with English-computed vectors works better than with target-language vectors.
numbers: Languages: French, German, Dutch, Mandarin. In the appendix, 20-40 percent of layers allowed successful steering on average. Success means the generated sentence contains the target word. Exact rates not extracted.
limits: Open-ended multi-token generation. Disagrees with Wendler et al., who found a language-neutral concept space at single-token level.
agent_relevance: A scaffold step written in English may steer more reliably than the same step in the user's language. Cheap to test.

source: Schut, Gal, Farquhar (2025) Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English? (word classes)
finding: The English route is partial. In 'Le bateau naviguait en douceur sur l'', the nouns eau, lac and soleil are chosen in English first. Non-lexical words do not route through English.
numbers: Qualitative logit-lens figure plus aggregate analysis.
limits: Exact rates not extracted.
agent_relevance: If the pivot is for content words, a restated problem should keep its content words in English.

source: Zhong, Cheng, Liu, Jiang, Wan, Chu, Murawaki, Kurohashi (2024) Beyond English-Centric LLMs: What Language Do Multilingual Language Models Think in?
finding: The latent language depends on the training mix. Llama2 uses English only. Swallow (English plus Japanese continued pretraining) and LLM-jp (balanced) use both English and Japanese internally.
numbers: Three Japanese-processing models, logit lens; also questions with cultural conflict between latent and output language. Numbers are in figures, not extracted.
limits: Japanese only. Descriptive; no behavioural difference shown.
agent_relevance: The pivot language is a product of the data mix. Pick the scaffold language per model.

source: Etxaniz, Azkune, Soroa, Lopez de Lacalle, Artetxe (2023) Do Multilingual Language Models Think Better in English?
finding: Self-translate (the model first translates the input to English, then answers) beats answering directly in the source language. Models do not use their full multilingual ability in non-English prompts.
numbers: Mean accuracy over 5 tasks, direct versus self-translate. XGLM 7.5B 40.1 vs 42.3 (+2.2). LLaMA 13B 40.6 vs 43.4 (+2.8). LLaMA 30B 43.1 vs 46.6 (+3.5). Smallest XGLM 39.6 vs 39.9 (+0.3). Tasks: XStoryCloze, XCOPA, XNLI, PAWS-X, MGSM.
limits: Larger models and high-resource languages gain more. External MT is still better, gap shrinks with size. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A restate step in a canonical language raised mean accuracy by 2 to 3.5 points. Nearest tested relative of a restate-the-message step.

source: Etxaniz, Azkune, Soroa, Lopez de Lacalle, Artetxe (2023) Do Multilingual Language Models Think Better in English? (per task, LLaMA 30B)
finding: Gains vary by task. XNLI +6.5, PAWS-X +4.7, XCOPA +3.2, XStoryCloze +2.3, MGSM +0.8. Self-translate on MGSM is flat for small LLaMA models because they solve almost no problems.
numbers: LLaMA 30B direct to self-translate: XNLI 37.0 to 43.5, PAWS-X 50.9 to 55.6, XCOPA 55.2 to 58.4, XStoryCloze 56.7 to 59.0, MGSM 15.5 to 16.3.
limits: Gains are strongest on sentence-pair tasks, weakest on multi-step math.
agent_relevance: A restate step helps comprehension-heavy items more than step-heavy items.

source: Shi et al. (2022) Language Models are Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoners
finding: MGSM: 250 grade-school math problems translated into 10 typologically diverse languages. Chain-of-thought emerges with scale in every language. English reasoning steps (EN-CoT) are as good as or better than steps in the question's language.
numbers: PaLM-540B: average over 4 underrepresented languages 44.9 percent versus 47.9 percent over 6 high-resource languages, a 3 point gap, though some languages are under 0.01 percent of training data. Best setting averaged 55 percent.
limits: Maths only. Greedy decoding. 6 exemplars. Training frequency was not a strong predictor.
agent_relevance: Reasoning transfers across languages; the language of the steps matters by a few points at most.

source: Shi et al. (2022) Language Models are Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoners (translate-test)
finding: Translate-EN (external translation, then solve) gave results similar to Native-CoT and EN-CoT for PaLM-540B on all languages, even Bengali and Swahili.
numbers: Thai, Telugu and Bengali reasoning on par with French, Japanese and Chinese.
limits: 2022 model; maths only.
agent_relevance: At frontier scale an explicit translation step is not clearly needed.

source: BICAUSE authors (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
finding: BICAUSE is a bilingual Chinese-English causal-chain set with forward and reversed chains. Models show language-specific attention. Chinese attends to causes and sentence-initial connectives; English spreads attention. A forward-order prior is applied rigidly to Chinese reversed chains.
numbers: Qwen1.5-1.8B-Chat forward chains: English 91.0 percent, Chinese 91.2 percent. Reversed chains: English 88.5 percent, Chinese 76.5 percent. SVCCA similarity: Chinese pair 0.73 in one comparison, English forward-reversed 0.64, Chinese forward-reversed about 0.46.
limits: Small item counts (about 50 per domain cell, 8 domains). Large Qwen models (14B, 72B) show about 97 percent in both languages, so the gap closes with scale. The 'relativity' label is a data-prior effect.
agent_relevance: Word order of the same content moved a small model's accuracy by 12 points, with size depending on language. Argues for canonical reordering before reasoning, at least for small models.

source: BICAUSE authors (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs (scale and paraphrase)
finding: Language gaps shrink with scale. On paraphrased data Qwen1.5-14B gets 97.5 in both languages and Qwen1.5-72B 97.0 and 96.2. On the original (non-paraphrased) table, small Llama-3.2 models are erratic: 1B scores 61.0 (En) vs 49.8 (Zh); 3B scores 27.0 (En) vs 56.8 (Zh).
numbers: Qwen1.5-1.8B paraphrased: English 88.5, Chinese 76.8. Qwen1.5-32B English 90.5 with one domain at 46.0.
limits: Different model families disagree on which language is easier. Tests per cell are small.
agent_relevance: Language effects are model-specific, so any rule from one model should be re-measured on ours.

source: Farina, Ballatore, McGillivray (2025) Mapping Meaning in Latin with LLMs: preverbed motion verbs and spatial relations
finding: GPT-4, Llama and Mistral were tested on Latin motion events: spotting preverbed motion verbs, labelling Source, Goal and Path relations, and disambiguating relation type. GPT-4 is best. Small models say 'yes' to almost everything.
numbers: Literal-motion subset, GPT-4: Goal F1 about 0.82, Path best F1 0.79 (two-shot), Source 0.77 (one-shot). Small Llama: recall 1.00 but precision 0.19-0.26, F1 0.33-0.41.
limits: Latin only. Annotation task, not a Talmy typology test. Imbalanced, small dataset. Errors came from salience over syntax and from linking proper nouns to the governing verb.
agent_relevance: Models can be prompted to extract Source, Goal and Path slots but over-label. An event-slot step needs a precision check.

source: Farina, Ballatore, McGillivray (2025) Mapping Meaning in Latin with LLMs: preverbed motion verbs and spatial relations (prompting)
finding: More shots did not fix over-labelling by small models. They tagged nearly everything as Goal, so F1 stayed 0.33-0.41 across settings, while GPT-4 held 0.82 on the same label.
numbers: Llama small: precision 0.19-0.26, recall 1.00. GPT-4 Goal F1 0.82.
limits: One dataset, one language.
agent_relevance: Report precision and recall separately for slot extraction, never F1 alone.

source: Mahowald et al. (2024) Dissociating language and thought in large language models
finding: Separates formal linguistic competence (rules and patterns) from functional competence (using language to reason about the world). LLMs are strong at the first and spotty at the second.
numbers: Review across many benchmarks; no single effect size.
limits: Position paper grounded in neuroscience. Tests no Whorf effects.
agent_relevance: Fluent wording is not evidence of sound thought. Treat wording effects as surface effects first.

source: Abdou et al. (2021) Can Language Models Encode Perceptual Structure Without Grounding? A Case Study in Color
finding: Text-only BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA colour-term embeddings align with the perceptual CIELAB space, by RSA and linear mapping. Larger models align better, and warm colours align better than cool ones.
numbers: RSA over 18 colour terms. Significant correlations in all configurations. Permuting the colour centroids gives non-significant results (p above 0.05). A low-dimensional subspace explains much of the variance.
limits: English only. Small sample. No cross-language test.
agent_relevance: Language statistics alone carry some perceptual structure. Background only.

source: Human Language Shapes the Emerging Physical Reasoning in Large Language Models (2026)
finding: Frames LLM physical reasoning as a machine linguistic-relativity effect. Frontier models rank molecular conformers near specialised force-field accuracy but follow a hydrogen-bond rule of thumb from the literature even when it reverses the true order.
numbers: 28 LLMs, 810 conformers, 27 molecules. Exact accuracies not read.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened. 'Linguistic relativity' is a metaphor for inherited text bias, not Whorf's claim.
agent_relevance: Model reasoning inherits the rules of thumb of its source text, not only the wording of the prompt.

source: Srinivas, Englhardt, Iyer, Patel (2025) Thinking While Speaking: Inference-Time Knowledge Transfer for Responsive Conversational Voice Agents
finding: Name overlap only. A small Talker model speaks while a frontier Reasoner thinks in parallel, and the Talker folds streamed results into its speech.
numbers: 290,571 synthetic examples, 6 domains, 7 small models (135M to 1.7B). Accuracy within 6.3 percent of the frontier Reasoner. User study n = 18.
limits: Engineering paper with no link to Slobin's work.
agent_relevance: A fast speaker plus slow thinker pattern. Low relevance to the schema.

source: Yang, Peng, Lee, Liu (2026) Think-Before-Speak: From Internal Evaluation to Public Expression in Multi-Agent Social Simulation
finding: Name overlap only. Agents keep a private structured state (dissonance, opinion climate, isolation risk, response strategy, willingness to speak) and an orchestrator picks one public utterance.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite and Gemini-2.5-Flash agents; traces varied across turn-allocation, silence and memory conditions. No accuracy figure.
limits: Social simulation with no ground truth.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping private reasoning out of the final message. Low relevance.

source: Zelikman, Harik, Shao, Jayasiri, Haber, Goodman (2024) Quiet-STaR: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Think Before Speaking
finding: Name overlap. The model learns to write an internal rationale at each token before predicting the next. Zero-shot gains with no task fine-tuning, after continued pretraining.
numbers: GSM8K 5.9 to 10.9 percent. CommonsenseQA 36.3 to 47.2 percent.
limits: Needs training; not a prompt scaffold.
agent_relevance: Cannot be used by us (no training). Confirms that hidden thinking before output helps.

source: Search note: no LLM study of Slobin-style thinking for speaking found
finding: No paper found that tests LLMs on Slobin's paradigm (event description in verb-framed versus satellite-framed languages, with attention or memory measures). The arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex searches hit rate limits and the WebSearch budget ran out, so the gap is not proven.
numbers: 0 relevant papers found.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search. Recheck when budgets refill.
agent_relevance: Treat as an open question. Do not assume a measured effect.

source: Search snippet: satellite- versus verb-framing underpredicts nonverbal motion categorisation (large language sample and simulations)
finding: A search result summary said a large cross-language study finds framing type predicts nonverbal motion categorisation less well than the original theory implies. Not opened; the link was not verified to be this paper.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Would be the human baseline for any LLM comparison. Open it before use.

source: Slobin (1996) From 'thought and language' to 'thinking for speaking'
finding: Original statement: while building a message, speakers attend to the features their language forces them to encode. Not opened in this run.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: From memory only.
agent_relevance: The model analogue is that the output language or format forces attention to certain slots (tense, number, path). A scaffold could make those slots explicit.

source: Abdou et al. (2021) size and corpus effects
finding: Alignment of colour-term embeddings with perceptual space rises with model size across four sizes. Corpus statistics of colour terms in Common Crawl help predict which colours align.
numbers: Baselines in the paper: fastText and PMI give weaker but non-zero alignment. Permuted controls non-significant.
limits: BERT-family, English only; exact per-size values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Background only. Wording statistics carry structure, so how a thing is usually described can shape what a model treats as similar.
